To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

a plug-in estimation procedure based on dimension reduction, additional thresholding, and Lepski’smethod is minimax optimal up to a logarithm in the sense that it attains the optimal rates of convergence over a wide rangeof classes of slope functions, covariance operators, and designs.

the adaptive estimator is minimax optimal up to a logarithm in the case of pointwise estimation and local averages, and that the minimax risk in this case is of order \(n^{-2/3} \) for Hölder slope functions and of order \(n^{-(\beta +1)/2\beta +1}\) for \(\beta \) -Hölder slope functions.

a data-driven choice of tuning parameters for a plug-in estimator of the slope parameter can be based on Lepski’s method and that the resulting estimator is adaptive with regard to the minimax risk over a wide range ofslope function classes and covariance operators.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a fully data-driven adaptive estimation procedure for linear functionals of the slope function in functional linear models.
the development of a data-driven procedure for the estimation of the slope parameter of the model that achieves the minimax optimal rate of convergence up to some logarithmic factor.
the estimation of the slope of a functional regression model in a non-parametric framework, where the functional regressors are observed on a finite number of equidistant points.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
adaptive estimation is possible in functional linear regression models with a linear functional response.
we can achieve optimal rates of convergence without any prior knowledge of the slope function or the covariance operator, and that we can estimate local averages as well.

the combination of Lepski’s method with model selection provides a powerful and flexible adaptive procedure for the estimation of linear functionalfunctionals in functional linear regression.
